source.title: Single Direction vs Low-Rank Refusal in Small LLMs

record.tranche_reason: The post applies the difference-in-means refusal-vector extraction and projection-ablation approach, and reports refusal-related outcomes on several models. It also tests weight orthogonalization and multi-vector variants.
record.gate_note: The post also reports implementation-choice comparisons, including batched versus sequential extraction and semantically matched versus generic prompt pairs. Those comparisons are described qualitatively or used to characterize extraction, so they are not included as additional behavioral outcome rows. Results cited from earlier work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The post replicates difference-in-means refusal-direction extraction and projection ablation on Qwen-1.8B-Chat, the original paper's model and method. It extends this to six more small models and adds weight orthogonalization with one or several stacked directions. Its own compliance and coherence results bear on V1, V2 and V4. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author finds two structures among small (<10B) models. In Qwen, gemma and LLaMA-3.1-8B one direction removes most refusal with little damage. In LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B (and partly phi-3) refusal looks like a low-rank subspace, where stacking a few directions helps but more costs coherence. The author frames this as pattern exploration in small models, not a general claim.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original difference-in-means refusal-vector extraction and projection-ablation idea, but generates semantically matched harmful/safe prompt pairs, compares extraction choices, tests additional models, and also orthogonalizes model weights and stacks multiple vectors.
record.method_sensitivity: Model choice changes how well a single direction works. For LLaMA-3.2-1B, the selected layers and number of stacked vectors change compliance and coherence; for LLaMA-3.2-3B, compliance continues to rise at k=5 while coherence declines. The post reports a small layer 7–10 dip in batched-versus-sequential vector similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal vectors from batched and sequential extraction have cosine similarity >95% across most layers of Qwen-1.8B, with a dip around layers 7–10. Sequential extraction and semantically matched pairs give marginally higher scores.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The difference-in-means refusal direction is robust to extraction choices (batching, matched vs. generic prompt pairs).

record.problems: The author says compliance and coherence scores come from an external LLM judge on a discrete scale and are approximate, with noise and non-determinism. Most rollouts use 100 harmful prompts; the 500-prompt dataset is used for the final confirmation. The author also notes limited dataset coverage, small model sizes (under 10B parameters), and omitted implementation details and benchmark tables. No error bars or statistical uncertainty estimates are reported in the post.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts is not tested. Benchmark numbers are given only for Qwen-1.8B (~1%). For LLaMA-3.1-8B the post says only 'minimal' degradation, with no numbers. Baseline refusal rates of the unmodified models are not reported.
Weight-edit results with numbers are reported only for LLaMA-3.2-1B and 3B. It is unclear whether the cross-model table (Qwen, gemma, LLaMA-8B) used runtime ablation or weight edits.
Affine and cone formulations are not tested. Multi-vector edits are not tried on the single-direction models.

missing.what: Cross-layer cosine-similarity heatmaps. Qwen and LLaMA-8B directions stabilize in mid-late layers; LLaMA-3.2-1B directions align only with nearby layers. This is the author's main structural evidence for single-direction vs. low-rank models.
The post states best single-layer compliance of ~25–26% on the 500-prompt set, versus ~21%/~19% on the 100-prompt set, and notes the 15% vs 19% discrepancy for 3B.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 'challenges' label is changed to limits_scope, because the rows are partial (15–39%) and no unmodified baseline is stated. The reader's V2 'supports' label is dropped: compliance of 0.16–0.26 after weight edits does not show that refusal is removed. All scores come from a DeepSeek judge on a {0, 0.5, 1} scale, with no uncertainty reported. 'Best' is chosen by compliance × coherence.

versions.untested_parts: The post tests removal with single-vector projection ablation, but not adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests. Capability preservation is checked only with the stated coherence and benchmark measures, not across general abilities.
Weight orthogonalization is tested on the named models, but the post does not report distribution or use of released edited checkpoints beyond these experiments.
No jailbreak mechanism suppressing the direction, or training against its ablation, is tested.
The post tests whether single vectors or stacked vectors work better and describes low-rank structure; it does not test affine or cone formulations.
No separate harmfulness judgment representation is measured.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test is reported.
The post does not vary how or when refusal is trained.

source_check.reason: Single direction gives ~39%, ~21% and ~15% (or ~19%) compliance, and k=1 weight edits give 0.158-0.262. Removal is incomplete. It is not shown absent, since no baseline is given.

relationships.reason: The weight edit keeps coherence at ~0.94–0.98 (r13, r25). But it raises compliance only to 0.16–0.37 even with 3–5 stacked vectors (r12, r18, r24, r30, r32). Stacking 15 vectors cuts coherence to 0.818 (r23).
relationships.display_finding: Weight editing retained approximately 0.94–0.98 coherence but achieved only 0.16–0.37 compliance even with 3–5 stacked vectors, while stacking 15 vectors reduced coherence to 0.818.

source_check.label: limits_scope

relationships.reason: Stacking 3–4 directions raises compliance over the best single direction: 0.251→0.373 for 1B and 0.262→0.344/0.374 for 3B (r11, r12, r18, r24, r30, r32).
relationships.display_finding: Stacking 3–4 directions raised compliance from 0.251 to 0.373 in 1B and from 0.262 to 0.344 or 0.374 in 3B.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-3.2-1B with k=5 or k=15; and models where one direction suffices
relationships.reason: For 1B, compliance falls at k=5 (0.298) and k=15 (0.334), while coherence drops to 0.818 (r20–r23). Even the subspace stays below ~37%. In Qwen, gemma and LLaMA-8B a single direction suffices (r4–r7), so multi-direction structure is model-dependent.
relationships.display_finding: Compliance fell to 0.298 and 0.334 at ranks 5 and 15, coherence dropped to 0.818, and subspace compliance remained below approximately 37%, while one direction sufficed in Qwen, gemma, and LLaMA-8B.

reader_labels.label: supports
